questions.q: What is a text embedding, precisely?
options: A compressed ZIP archive of the original text
A dense numeric vector produced by a neural network, representing a piece of text's meaning as a point in high-dimensional space
A list of the most frequent words in a document
A hash value used only for detecting exact duplicate text
questions.explain: Embeddings are dense, meaning-bearing vectors, not compression artifacts, word-frequency lists, or hashes for exact matching.

questions.q: In this lesson's worked example, why do "a dog barking in the yard" and "a puppy barking outside" get nearly identical embeddings?
options: They share the exact same words
They are the same length in characters
They mean nearly the same thing, and embeddings capture meaning rather than exact shared vocabulary
The embedding model memorized this specific sentence pair during training
questions.explain: Despite sharing almost no exact words, the two phrases are semantically similar, and that similarity is what the embedding model captures as nearby vector positions.

questions.q: What does 'dimensionality' refer to for an embedding?
options: How many documents are stored in the vector database
The physical size of the server running the model
How many numbers make up each embedding vector
The number of languages the model supports
questions.explain: Dimensionality is simply the length of the vector — common real-world sizes include 384, 768, 1024, 1536, and 3072.

questions.q: Does any single dimension of a real embedding correspond to one human-readable concept, like 'dog-ness'?
options: No — meaning is distributed across the whole vector, learned automatically during training, not hand-assigned to individual dimensions
Yes, every model documents which dimension maps to which concept
Yes, but only for the first ten dimensions
Only for embeddings under 100 dimensions
questions.explain: Embedding dimensions are not hand-designed to represent specific human concepts; the meaning is spread across the full vector in a way the model learns on its own.

questions.q: Why can't you meaningfully compare a vector from one embedding model to a vector from a different embedding model?
options: Different models always produce vectors of different lengths, making comparison impossible
It is actually fine to compare vectors from any two models
Each model defines its own embedding space based on its own training, so the same coordinates mean something different in each one
Comparing vectors requires paying an extra licensing fee
questions.explain: An embedding space is entirely a product of how its specific model was trained; two different models place the same concept at different coordinates, so cross-model comparisons are meaningless even when vector lengths happen to match.
